title: Ramprasad's Ledger
hookLine: a clerk's account book fills up with songs to Kali
carry: god as ma: a child may bring her anything
tomorrow: Humbler Than a Blade of Grass
last: THE MOTHER WHO BINDS AND FREES.

cards: An office in Calcutta. A young clerk is supposed to be copying figures into the account book, rows of numbers, day after day.

But the other clerks notice the margins of his ledger filling up with something else: lines of verse, songs to Kali, the dark Mother. Somebody takes the book to the employer, expecting the young man to be fired.
The employer opens it, starts reading, and doesn't stop. Today, the Shakta stream through one singer: Ramprasad Sen.

teach.b: Tradition says the employer was so moved that instead of dismissing him, he sent Ramprasad home to his village with an allowance, so he could do nothing but sing.
His songs spread from village to village, and tradition gives a melody his name. Listen to how he talks to Kali. Not like a courtier bowing to a queen.
Like a child to his mother. In one song, in paraphrase, he complains: other children have a mother who looks after them, so why am I left like this? Is this how a mother behaves?
He sulks, he pleads, he threatens to tell everyone. That's the Shakta teaching at its warmest: God as Ma.

teach.h: A CHILD, CROSS WITH HIS MOTHER
teach.b: The Goddess may be fierce, with a sword and a necklace of heads, but to her child she is Mother, and a child may bring her anything, even a complaint. People tell a story about him.
He was mending a fence and needed someone to hold the rope on the other side. His young daughter came and held it. Later, when he thanked her, she said she'd been away the whole time.
So who held the rope? In the story, the Mother herself, wearing a little girl's face. And his songs aren't only sweet.
In one, he scolds his own mind as a lazy farmer: this human life is a good field, and you've left it lying fallow. Tend it, and gold would grow. Tender with the Mother, hard on himself.
That's the voice that came out of an account book.

how: Ramprasad's songs to Kali are sung in Bengal at Kali Puja, at home and in devotional gatherings, as part of the song tradition known as Shyama Sangeet.

games.q: what does “bengal's shakta and vaishnava streams” mean?
o: two kinds of temple dance performed in Calcutta
Bengal's old schools of logic and grammar in Nabadwip
Bengal's devotion to Ma and to Krishna, sung more than argued

p: held by the Mother, in the story

s: in the story, Ramprasad is fired for writing songs at work
tradition says his employer sent him home with an allowance, so he could sing.
Ramprasad speaks to Kali like a child cross with his mother
he complains, pleads and sulks, because she is Ma.
his songs are only gentle and sweet
he also scolds his own mind as a lazy farmer who left a good field fallow.

games.q: you're Ramprasad's employer. a clerk's ledger is full of songs to Kali instead of figures. what do you do?
o: send him home with an allowance to sing.
tell him to keep the songs at home.
games.why: tradition says the employer read on, was moved, and gave him an allowance so he could do nothing but sing.

practice: Picture your day as a small plot of ground: some of it planted, some lying fallow, a thing you keep meaning to start, a call you haven't made. Notice it without scolding yourself.
Then, if you pray, tell the Mother, or God, exactly how you feel about it, complaint and all, the way Ramprasad did. If you don't, say it honestly to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams: the Shakta stream in Ramprasad Sen, the clerk who filled his ledger with songs and talked to Kali like a child to his mother. Today's word.
